source_packet.title: From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology: A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education
source_packet.evidence:
methods: Conceptual synthesis of learning sciences and the staged-use GRAIT framework for formal education.
interpretation: AI support should follow demonstrated learning readiness, rather than replace foundational thinking from the outset.
limitations: This paper proposes a conceptual instructional framework; it does not experimentally establish that staged AI access improves outcomes.
approach: Conceptual synthesis of learning sciences and the staged-use GRAIT framework for formal education.
explain: A proposed staged approach to AI use in formal learning; distinguish foundational independent work from guided and selective offloading.
limitation: This paper proposes a conceptual instructional framework; it does not experimentally establish that staged AI access improves outcomes.

source_packet.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
source_packet.evidence:
findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear b
methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were cod
interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal media
limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.
finding: Tailored agents increased enjoyment and reduced boredom relative to ChatGPT; emotional scaffolding also strengthened observed task-level regulation. Immediate learning gains occurred in all groups, without a statistically significant advantage for the tailored agents.
approach: Preregistered three-arm classroom experiment (144 students; 48 per condition) comparing ChatGPT, an SRL-supporting chatbot and an emotionally supportive SRL chatbot; 85 completed a four-week follow-up.
explain: In a randomized high-school trial, adding self-regulation prompts and emotional support changed how students felt and engaged during the task, but did not establish superior knowledge or transfer gains.
limitation: A single 25-minute intervention, attrition at follow-up, and weak reliability in some knowledge tests limit the learning and retention claims.

source_packet.title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
source_packet.evidence:
findings: The 51 included studies yielded four overlapping domains: metacognition/self-regulated learning (Lai et al., 2026) , trust (El Hosayny et al., 2026) , human-AI co-regulation/collaboration (Zakaria et al., 2025) , and AI literacy/learner agency (El Hosayny et al., 2026) . Because studies could address multiple constructs, these counts are overlapping contributions and should not be summed. The following sections synthesize evidence within and across these domains. The five research questions are addressed by integrating the empirical evidence synthesized in Section 4 with the theoretical interpretation developed in Sections 5.1-5.3 (Table 2 ). The synthesis indicates that the educational valu
methods: This study employed a theory-building systematic review to synthesize empirical evidence on the psychological processes underlying generative-AI-supported foreign language learning. The review followed PRISMA 2020 for study identification, screening, and reporting and used qualitative thematic and conceptual synthesis to develop a theoretical account. The review focused on three interconnected mechanisms: metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-reg
interpretation: This systematic review examined the psychological processes through which learners engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in foreign language education. Drawing on 51 empirical studies, it moved beyond whether GenAI improves particular language skills to examine how learners understand, evaluate, regulate, and coordinate their interactions with generative systems. Metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation emerged as interco
limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. The 51 studies varied substantially in participants, research designs, learning contexts, AI applications, and operationalization's of psychological constructs, which limits direct comparison across studies. Moreover, the evidence base is relatively recent and rapidly evolving; findings associated with particular GenAI systems may therefore change as technologies and patterns of use develop. The review has methodological limitations related to its singleauthor design. Screening, full-text assessment, and thematic coding were conducted by the sole author without independent review
explain: This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning.
limitation: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings.

source_packet.title: Between cognitive offloading and critical autonomy: a systematic review of the epistemic implications of generative AI in higher education
source_packet.evidence:
findings: Although several included studies initially focused on educational performance domains such as writing assistance, formative assessment, or learning efficiency, they were retained in the synthesis when their findings directly addressed epistemic processes related to knowledge validation, cognitive delegation, authorship, information trustworthiness, evaluative judgment, or learner autonomy in AI-mediated environments. Eligibility decisions therefore prioritized epistemic implications rather than disciplinary context alone. A total of 26 studies were included in the final synthesis. The included evidence demonstrated a marked temporal concentration in the period 2025-2026, indicating that res
methods: A systematic review with thematic and framework synthesis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021) . The review was restricted to original empirical studies employing qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods designs. A meta-analysis was not considered appropriate because the included studies examined heterogeneous populations, educati
interpretation: The current empirical evidence indicates that generative AI can support feedback, conceptual clarification, reflective inquiry, and self-regulated learning when its use is structured around explanation, comparison, verification, and metacognitive reflection. Study selection, data extraction, and methodological appraisal were conducted independently by two reviewers; the corpus included qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, quasi-experimental, and randomized designs; and the geographical distribution provided substantial representation from Global South higher education contexts. draft.headline: Comparing AI Integration Strategies in Education
draft.deck: Three studies explore different approaches to integrating AI in education, from a staged introduction in formal settings to gradual normalization in higher education. Meanwhile, a systematic review and a writing study highlight the psychological and practical impacts of AI, raising questions about long-term engagement and ethical concerns.
draft.letter: In the first study, an essay proposes a staged approach to integrating AI in formal education, suggesting that AI support should follow demonstrated learning readiness. In contrast, a study in higher education found that gradual normalization of AI use led to increased uptake and positive attitudes, but raised ethical concerns. Another study examined the effects of prompt-based emotional scaffolding versus general-purpose chatbot interaction, finding that emotional support improved enjoyment and task-level performance. However, a systematic review highlighted the psychological processes underlying GenAI interactions, while a writing study found that AI-supported writing did not correlate with strong independent performance. These studies raise questions about the long-term impacts and ethical considerations of AI in education.

tension.title: Long-Term Effects of AI Integration in Education
tension.text: While studies suggest that gradual normalization of AI use in higher education can lead to increased uptake and positive attitudes, the long-term effects and ethical considerations remain unresolved. Similarly, the systematic review highlights the psychological processes underlying GenAI interactions, but the rapid evolution of GenAI technologies and the variability in study designs limit the conclusions. How do these approaches affect sustained attention and learning in the long term, and what are the ethical implications of AI-supported learning?

signals.title: Comparing Staged Use of AI in Formal Education vs. Gradual Normalization in Higher Education
signals.text: The first source, an abstract-only essay, proposes a staged approach to integrating AI in formal education, suggesting that AI support should follow demonstrated learning readiness, rather than replace foundational thinking from the outset. The second source describes a study in higher education where students gradually normalized AI use, leading to increased uptake and more positive attitudes, but raised ethical concerns about the authenticity of learning. Both approaches aim to integrate AI, but the first is more cautious, advocating for a gradual introduction based on readiness, while the second suggests a natural integration over time, though with ongoing ethical scrutiny.

In contrast, S6 showed that generative AI technostress was negatively associated with both learning engagement and academic adaptability, suggesting that technostress hinders these outcomes. Both studies highlight the importance of emotional support and adaptability in learning, but S2's one-time intervention and S6's cross-sectional design limit the conclusions about long-term effects and causal relationships.

signals.title: Synthesizing Evidence on Metacognition and Trust in AI-Assisted Learning vs. Cognitive Offloading in Writing
signals.text: A theory-building systematic review (S3) on metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning (S3) contrasts with a study (S7) on layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in AI-assisted writing. S3 highlights the psychological processes underlying GenAI interactions, emphasizing metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation. S7, on the other hand, examines the quality of AI-supported and independent no-AI writing, finding that AI-supported products did not correlate with strong independent performance. S3's limitations include the variability in study designs and the rapid evolution of GenAI technologies, while S7's limitations include the confounding of conditions with classes and the limited scope of near transfer in Week 8 assessments.
